title: Forty-Five Chromosomes: Monosomy X, Turner Karyotypes and Robertsonian Carriers
summary: Why 45,X is the only viable monosomy, which karyotypes cause Turner syndrome and what Y material means, and why a balanced Robertsonian carrier also has 45 chromosomes yet is usually healthy.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 71 Hits 1, 6 and 7 and Exam Traps 3 and 4. Checked against the 2024 international Turner syndrome guideline (Gravholt 2024), Yang 2017, Cheng 2025, Jackson 2018 and Zhao 2015. Hit 6’s karyotype percentages (45,X 50%, i(Xq) 20%, mosaics 10%, deletions/rings/Y 15%) differ from the guideline’s Table 1; the lesson teaches the guideline figures (register flag rv-turner-karyotype-mix). Hit 6’s Y-material risk is qualified: rates vary widely and gonadectomy is individualised (rv-turner-y-gonadectomy). Hit 7’s “21;21 → 100% Down or nonviable” is qualified by rare trisomy rescue (rv-rob2121-rescue). Not taught: Turner height (<150 cm) and other clinical features beyond the hook, the Number Vault’s “>95% of 45,X conceptions lost” (Yang 2017 gives ~1% surviving, consistent), Down syndrome origin percentages (Hit 2).

objectives: Explain why 45,X is the only monosomy compatible with live birth and why 45,Y and autosomal monosomies are not.
List the main karyotypes of Turner syndrome with their approximate frequencies and state the laboratory approach to mosaicism and Y material.
Explain why a balanced Robertsonian carrier has 45 chromosomes yet is usually healthy, and predict the reproductive outcomes of heterologous and homologous carriers.

scenes.title: Three chromosome counts
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three karyotype reports on the cytogenetics bench. (1) A newborn girl with neck webbing and puffy hands and feet: 45,X. (2) A healthy woman referred after two miscarriages: 45,XX,der(13;14)(q10;q10). (3) A child with features of Down syndrome: 46 chromosomes, including a der(21;21) fused chromosome. Question token: “Two count 45, one counts 46. Which is healthy, and why?”

cues.text: Three karyotype reports. A newborn girl with a webbed neck and swollen hands and feet: forty-five chromosomes, one X.
A healthy woman with two miscarriages: also forty-five, with chromosomes 13 and 14 joined. And a child with Down syndrome features who has forty-six.
Two counts of forty-five, one of forty-six. Which person is healthy, and why does the count mislead?

scenes.title: Why losing a chromosome is usually lethal
scenes.altText: Schematic: a row of chromosome pairs with one chromosome missing. Cards: any autosomal monosomy is embryonic lethal; 45,Y (no X at all) is early embryonic lethal; 45,X is the only monosomy compatible with live birth — yet only about 1% of conceptuses recognised with 45,X survive to birth; it has been hypothesised (not proven) that liveborn 45,X individuals carry a hidden normal cell line (cryptic mosaicism).

cues.text: Embryos with any autosomal monosomy do not survive, most likely because halving gene dose hurts sensitive genes and unmasks harmful recessive variants.
Losing the X is no better. A conceptus with only a Y chromosome, forty-five Y, dies early in embryonic life.
Forty-five X is the only monosomy compatible with live birth, and even then only about one percent of conceptuses with this karyotype survive to birth.
Some experts suspect that liveborn forty-five X individuals all carry a hidden normal cell line, a cryptic mosaic, but there is no conclusive proof.

scenes.title: Turner syndrome is not one karyotype
scenes.altText: Karyotype bar (2024 international Turner guideline, Table 1): 45,X 40–50%; 45,X/46,XX mosaic 15–25%; 46,X,i(Xq) or idic(Xp) about 15%; 45,X/46,XY 10–12%; 45,X/47,XXX mosaics about 3%; ring X and unbalanced X-autosome translocations rare. Definition card: a phenotypic female with one intact X and complete or partial absence of the second sex chromosome, plus typical clinical features. Testing card: count at least 30 metaphases on a chromosome analysis as first-line (detects about 10% mosaicism with 95% confidence); rapid methods (microarray, FISH, PCR) when speed matters, confirmed by karyotype. Y-material card: Y material is associated with gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma; reported rates vary widely; search for Y material by PCR in 45,X individuals with virilisation, not in all 45,X; decisions on gonadectomy are individualised.

cues.text: Turner syndrome means one intact X plus complete or partial loss of the second sex chromosome, with typical clinical features. The 2024 guideline puts plain forty-five X at forty to fifty percent of cases.
The rest have other karyotypes: mosaics with a normal forty-six XX line in fifteen to twenty-five percent, an isochromosome of Xq in about fifteen, and a forty-six XY line in ten to twelve percent.

The guideline asks the lab to count at least thirty metaphases, which detects about ten percent mosaicism with ninety-five percent confidence. Microarray, FISH or PCR can give a rapid answer, confirmed by karyotype.

Y chromosome material is associated with gonadoblastoma, but reported rates vary widely. Look for hidden Y material by PCR when a forty-five X patient shows virilisation, and decide on gonadectomy case by case.

scenes.title: Robertsonian fusions: 45 and healthy
scenes.altText: Schematic: two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) fuse at the centromere; both long arms are kept, both short arms are lost, giving 45 chromosomes. Short-arm card: acrocentric short arms carry the nucleolar organiser regions (repeated ribosomal DNA), shared by all five acrocentrics, so losing two is compensated; carriers are usually phenotypically normal. Frequency card: about 1 in 1000 births; der(13;14) and der(14;21) make up about 85%. Reproduction card: a heterologous carrier can have normal or balanced-carrier children, but unbalanced gametes raise the risk of infertility, miscarriage, unbalanced offspring and uniparental disomy if 14 or 15 is involved. A homologous carrier such as der(21;21) makes only disomic or nullisomic gametes, so conceptuses are trisomic or monosomic, with a rare normal child after trisomy rescue. Hook answers: (1) Turner syndrome; (2) the healthy balanced carrier; (3) translocation Down syndrome with 46 chromosomes.

cues.text: In a Robertsonian translocation, two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at the centromere. Both long arms are kept, both short arms are lost, so the carrier has forty-five chromosomes.

The short arms hold repeated ribosomal RNA genes that all five acrocentrics share, so the loss is covered. Carriers are usually healthy. About one birth in a thousand carries one; 13 with 14 and 14 with 21 make up about eighty-five percent.

The problem comes at meiosis. Unbalanced gametes raise the risk of miscarriage and unbalanced children. A carrier of a 21 with 21 fusion makes only gametes with two or no copies of 21, so conceptions are trisomic or monosomic, apart from rare trisomy rescue.

Back to the hook. The newborn has Turner syndrome. The woman is the healthy one: a balanced carrier. The child has translocation Down syndrome, with forty-six chromosomes: the fused chromosome holds two copies of 21q, and a free 21 is added.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “45,Y is viable, like 45,X” (✓ 45,Y is early embryonic lethal; 45,X is the only viable monosomy); “Robertsonian carriers have 46 chromosomes” (✓ balanced carriers have 45; an unbalanced carrier with an extra free chromosome counts 46); “Turner syndrome always means 45,X” (✓ only 40–50%; mosaics, isochromosome Xq and Y-bearing lines make up the rest).

cues.text: Trap one: if forty-five X survives, forty-five Y should too. No: without an X the embryo dies early. Forty-five X is the only viable monosomy.
Trap two: a Robertsonian carrier has forty-six chromosomes. No: a balanced carrier has forty-five. It is the unbalanced child with an extra 21 who counts forty-six.
Trap three: Turner syndrome always means forty-five X. No: that is only forty to fifty percent of cases; the rest are mosaic or structural.

scenes.title: Count the chromosomes, then weigh the cargo
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Count the chromosomes, then weigh the cargo. A missing X is a missing truckload; a Robertsonian fusion only drops two short-arm trailers of spare ribosomal genes. Same count of 45, very different loss.” Tokens: 45,X = whole X missing · rob = spare rDNA lost · der(21;21) = trisomy or monosomy. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: count the chromosomes, then weigh the cargo. A missing X is a missing truckload. A Robertsonian fusion only drops two little trailers of spare ribosomal genes. Same count, very different loss.

Where it breaks: many people with Turner syndrome have forty-six chromosomes in some or all cells; a balanced carrier is healthy but can still have unbalanced children; and uniparental disomy can cause disease even when the count looks normal.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “45,X is the only viable monosomy · 45,Y and autosomal monosomies are lethal · Turner is 45,X in only 40–50%”, “Robertsonian balanced carrier = 45, usually healthy · der(21;21) → trisomy or monosomy conceptions”.

cues.text: A count of forty-five can mean Turner syndrome, the only viable monosomy, or a healthy balanced Robertsonian carrier whose lost short arms hold ribosomal genes shared with other acrocentrics, so always read the whole karyotype, not just the number.

props.label: 45,X only viable monosomy · 45,Y lethal · Turner 45,X in 40–50%

explanation.what: Plain language: people normally have 46 chromosomes. Missing a whole chromosome is almost always fatal before birth; the single exception is missing one X, which causes Turner syndrome. A different kind of 45 happens when two small chromosomes glue together end to end: almost nothing is lost, so the person is healthy but may have pregnancy losses or children with an extra chromosome. Scientific terms: monosomy, 45,X, cryptic mosaicism, isochromosome Xq [i(Xq)], isodicentric Xp, 45,X/46,XY mosaicism, gonadoblastoma, acrocentric chromosome, nucleolar organiser region (NOR), ribosomal DNA (rDNA), Robertsonian translocation (ROB), heterologous vs homologous ROB, der(21;21), uniparental disomy (UPD), trisomy rescue.
explanation.why: An autosomal monosomy reduces the dosage of haploinsufficient genes and unmasks recessive deleterious variants, which is thought to explain its lethality. In 45,X the remaining X is not inactivated, so mainly the genes that normally escape X inactivation are at half dose; even so, most 45,X conceptuses are lost. Acrocentric short arms carry mainly repeated rDNA shared by all five acrocentrics, so a Robertsonian fusion loses little, but meiosis in a carrier can produce unbalanced gametes.
explanation.measure: Turner karyotypes (2024 guideline): 45,X 40–50%; 45,X/46,XX 15–25%; i(Xq)/idic(Xp) ~15%; 45,X/46,XY 10–12%; 45,X/47,XXX mosaics ~3%; ring X rare. Count ≥30 metaphases first-line. PCR for Y material in 45,X with virilisation (not routine in all 45,X); individualised gonadectomy decisions. About 1% of 45,X conceptuses survive to birth. Robertsonian: about 1 in 1000 births; der(13;14) and der(14;21) ~85%; balanced carrier 45 chromosomes; about 5% of Down syndrome is due to a chromosome 21 translocation, about 95% of those Robertsonian.
explanation.differs: 45,X (whole X missing, Turner syndrome) vs balanced Robertsonian 45 (only short arms lost, usually healthy); heterologous ROB (normal, balanced or unbalanced offspring) vs homologous ROB such as der(21;21) (only trisomic or monosomic conceptions, rare rescue); balanced carrier 45 vs unbalanced translocation trisomy 46.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the only viable monosomy, reject 45,Y, give the chromosome count of a Robertsonian carrier and why they are healthy, recognise Turner mosaics and the significance of Y material, and predict recurrence for a der(21;21) parent.

mnemonic.text: Count the chromosomes, then weigh the cargo: a missing X is a missing truckload; a Robertsonian fusion only drops two short-arm trailers of spare ribosomal genes.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates a true monosomy from a fusion that lowers the count without losing unique genes.
mnemonic.limitation: Many people with Turner syndrome have 46 chromosomes in some or all cells (mosaics, i(Xq)); balanced carriers can have unbalanced children; uniparental disomy can cause disease with a normal-looking count.

analogyLimitations: Turner karyotype frequencies are guideline estimates; individual series differ.
takeaway: A count of forty-five can mean Turner syndrome, the only viable monosomy, or a healthy balanced Robertsonian carrier whose lost short arms hold ribosomal genes shared with other acrocentrics, so always read the whole karyotype, not just the number.

questions.stem: A karyotype is pending on a newborn girl with neck webbing and lymphoedema of the hands and feet. Which karyotype lacking one whole chromosome is compatible with survival to birth?

options.rationale: Correct. 45,X (Turner syndrome) is the only monosomy compatible with live birth, although only about 1% of 45,X conceptuses survive.
Incorrect. Complete loss of the X chromosome is early embryonic lethal.
Incorrect. Autosomal monosomies are embryonic lethal.
Incorrect. Autosomal monosomies are embryonic lethal; chromosome 16 is no exception.

questions.stem: A healthy woman referred after two miscarriages has the karyotype 45,XX,der(13;14)(q10;q10). Which statement best explains her result?

options.text: She is a balanced Robertsonian carrier; the lost short arms carry repeated ribosomal genes also present on other acrocentrics
options.rationale: Correct. Fusion of two acrocentrics keeps both long arms and lowers the count to 45; the lost short-arm material is compensated.

options.text: The count must be a laboratory error, because a healthy person always has 46 chromosomes
options.rationale: Incorrect. A balanced Robertsonian carrier has 45 chromosomes and is usually phenotypically normal.

options.text: She has a monosomy of chromosome 13 compatible with life
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both long arms of 13 and 14 are present on the fused chromosome; autosomal monosomies are lethal.
Incorrect. She has two X chromosomes; the missing count comes from the 13;14 fusion.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with Turner syndrome has the karyotype 45,X/46,XY. According to the 2024 international Turner syndrome guideline, what is the appropriate response to the Y material?

options.text: Individualised decision-making about gonadectomy, weighing gonadoblastoma/dysgerminoma risk against gonadal function and fertility
options.rationale: Correct. The guideline recommends individualised decisions, including timing, weighing gonadoblastoma/dysgerminoma risk against gonadal function and fertility; reported gonadoblastoma rates range from 0% to 100% across studies.

options.text: No action: Y material in Turner syndrome carries no tumour risk
options.rationale: Incorrect. Y material is associated with gonadoblastoma, with or without malignant transformation.
Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY; this patient has Turner syndrome with a 46,XY cell line, which the Turner guideline covers.

options.text: Repeat the karyotype because a Y line cannot occur in Turner syndrome
options.rationale: Incorrect. 45,X/46,XY accounts for about 10–12% of Turner karyotypes.

claims.text: 45,X is the only viable monosomy; autosomal monosomies and 45,Y are embryonic lethal; about 1% of 45,X conceptuses survive.
Cryptic mosaicism in liveborn 45,X is a hypothesis without conclusive evidence.
Turner definition and karyotype frequencies; ≥30 metaphases first-line; rapid methods confirmed by karyotype.
Y material and gonadoblastoma; PCR search only with virilisation; individualised gonadectomy decisions.
Robertsonian structure, 45 chromosomes, rDNA short arms, usually healthy, about 1/1000, der(13;14) and der(14;21) ~85%.
Heterologous and homologous carrier outcomes; trisomy rescue; translocation Down syndrome counts 46.
“Count the chromosomes, then weigh the cargo.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 71 Hit 6 gives Turner karyotypes as 45,X 50%, i(Xq) 20%, deletions/rings/Y 15%, mosaics 10%. The 2024 guideline (Gravholt 2024, Table 1) gives 45,X 40–50%, 45,X/46,XX 15–25%, i(Xq)/idic(Xp) ~15%, 45,X/46,XY 10–12%, 45,X/47,XXX ~3%, rings rare; the lesson teaches the guideline figures (register flag rv-turner-karyotype-mix).

Ch. 71 Hit 6 states that any Y material means gonadoblastoma risk, and the imported simulator explanation says it “warrants gonadectomy”. Gravholt 2024 reports gonadoblastoma rates from 0% to 100%, recommends PCR for Y material only in 45,X with virilisation, and recommends individualised gonadectomy decisions (register flag rv-turner-y-gonadectomy).

Ch. 71 Hit 7 says a 21;21 carrier has 100% Down syndrome offspring or nonviable conceptions. Zhao 2015 agrees that homologous carriers make only disomic or nullisomic gametes but notes an occasional phenotypically normal child by trisomy rescue (register flag rv-rob2121-rescue).

verification.notes: All 6 factual claims checked against Gravholt 2024, Yang 2017, Cheng 2025, Jackson 2018 and Zhao 2015 (full texts via Europe PMC). Independent fact-check pass re-verified citation metadata and every taught statement against these full texts; qualified the autosomal-monosomy mechanism (likely, not proven), described the der(21;21) karyotype without a full ISCN string, and softened meiotic-risk wording. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
